title: 🫧 Mixtures & Solutions Kitchen
description: Welcome to the Mixtures & Solutions Kitchen! You are a Grade 6 student running a special chemistry kitchen where you explore how substances mix, dissolve, and can be separated again. Over 14 weeks, you will learn the difference between pure and impure substances, master separation techniques like filtering and evaporation, and tackle real-world challenges like water purification. Handle chemical spills, investigate chromatography, and present your findings at the Lab Showcase. Can you become the Separation Specialist?
subject: chemistry
how_to_play: You are a Grade 6 student exploring mixtures and separation techniques over a 14-week chemistry lab program.
Each week presents a lab challenge with choices that affect your knowledge, safety, and creativity.
Watch your dashboard — your Lab Stations (Mixing, Filtering, Heating, Analysis, Purification) are interconnected.
NPCs like Professor Beaker (teacher), Bubble (lab mascot), Meera, and Sameer react to your decisions.
Random events like supply spills and guest scientists will test your adaptability.
Keep your Safety Compliance high — if it drops too low, you will lose lab privileges!
learning_objectives: Distinguish between pure substances and mixtures
Understand the process of dissolving and what makes a solution
Learn what saturation means and how temperature affects solubility
Master separation techniques: filtering, evaporation, distillation, chromatography, and magnetic separation
Practice safe laboratory procedures when handling chemicals
Apply separation knowledge to real-world problems like water purification
cultural_context: School chemistry laboratory, hands-on STEM learning, real-world water purification and food chemistry

rounds.round_title: Week 1: Welcome to the Mixtures Kitchen
rounds.situation: It is your first day in the Mixtures & Solutions Kitchen! The lab benches are filled with jars of salt, sand, iron filings, food coloring, oil, and water. Professor Beaker holds up a glass of clear liquid. 'Is this pure water, or is there something dissolved in it?' he asks. 'By the end of this course, you will be able to answer that question — and separate anything mixed together!' How do you want to start?
rounds.goal: Choose how to begin your exploration of mixtures and solutions.
rounds.coaching_moment: Delayed gratification: Learning the difference between pure and mixed substances now will be the foundation for every separation technique you master.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How can you tell if a clear liquid is pure water or has something dissolved in it?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 6 students entering a chemistry lab with colorful jars of salt, sand, iron filings, food coloring, oil and water on benches, teacher holding up a glass of clear liquid

choices.label: A. A mixture is two or more substances combined together that are not chemically joined
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A mixture is two or more substances physically combined together without any chemical reaction. The substances keep their own properties and can be separated again. For example, trail mix (nuts + raisins + chocolate) is a mixture — you can pick each part out. Air is a mixture of gases!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. A mixture is always a liquid where one substance dissolves in another
choices.feedback: 💡 Mixtures are not always liquids! A mixture can be solids (trail mix), liquids (salt water), gases (air), or combinations. Sand and iron filings is a solid mixture. Smoke is a mixture of gas and tiny solid particles. The key point is that the substances are combined but not chemically joined.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. Once substances are mixed together, they can never be separated again
choices.feedback: 💡 One of the most important things about mixtures is that they CAN be separated! Unlike chemical compounds, the substances in a mixture keep their individual properties. You can filter sand from water, evaporate water to get salt, or use a magnet to pull iron from sand.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. Pure substances and mixtures are the same thing because everything is made of atoms
choices.feedback: 💡 They are quite different! A pure substance contains only one type of particle (like pure water — only H2O molecules). A mixture contains two or more different substances that are not chemically bonded. Salt water is a mixture: it contains salt particles AND water molecules together.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.situation: Professor Beaker places ten substances on each bench — tap water, distilled water, orange juice, milk, sugar, salt, sand, iron filings, air in a balloon, and a copper coin. 'Sort these into PURE substances and MIXTURES,' he challenges. 'But be careful — some are not what they seem! Is air pure? Is milk a solution?' Sameer is already making a hypothesis chart.
rounds.goal: Classify substances as pure or mixtures and understand the difference.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Classification is a powerful scientific tool. Sorting things into categories reveals hidden patterns and connections.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Is air a pure substance or a mixture? What about orange juice? How can you tell?
rounds.image_prompt: Lab bench with ten labeled substances in jars and containers — water, juice, milk, sugar, salt, sand, iron filings, balloon, copper coin — students sorting and debating

choices.label: A. A homogeneous mixture looks the same throughout, while a heterogeneous mixture has visibly different parts
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ In a homogeneous mixture (like salt water), the composition is uniform — every spoonful is the same. In a heterogeneous mixture (like a salad or sand-and-gravel), you can see the different parts. 'Homo' means same, 'hetero' means different. Solutions are homogeneous mixtures!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. Heterogeneous mixtures are always liquids and homogeneous mixtures are always solids
choices.feedback: 💡 Both types can be solids, liquids, or gases! Salt water is a homogeneous liquid. Trail mix is a heterogeneous solid. Air is a homogeneous gas mixture. Muddy water is a heterogeneous liquid. What matters is whether the mixture looks uniform (homogeneous) or has visible different parts (heterogeneous).

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. You can always tell a mixture apart from a pure substance just by looking at it
choices.feedback: 💡 Homogeneous mixtures can look exactly like pure substances! Salt water looks identical to pure water. You would need to taste it, evaporate it, or test its boiling point to tell the difference. Heterogeneous mixtures (like sand in water) are easier to spot, but many mixtures are invisible to the eye.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. Milk is a pure substance because it looks the same throughout
choices.feedback: 💡 Milk looks uniform, but it is actually a mixture called a colloid! Under a microscope, you can see tiny fat droplets suspended in water. If you leave milk out, it separates — cream rises to the top. A colloid is a special type of mixture where tiny particles are evenly spread but do not dissolve.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: Professor Beaker stirs a spoonful of sugar into warm water. It disappears completely! 'This is a solution — the sugar has DISSOLVED in the water,' he says. 'The sugar is the solute, the water is the solvent, and together they make a solution. But can everything dissolve? Does the amount of water matter? Let us find out!' He places salt, sugar, sand, flour, and oil at each bench.
rounds.goal: Make solutions and understand dissolving, solutes, and solvents.
rounds.coaching_moment: Observation: Dissolving looks like the substance disappears, but it is still there — just broken into particles too small to see. Science often reveals hidden truths.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If you dissolve salt in water and the salt seems to disappear, where did it go? Is it really gone?
rounds.image_prompt: Student stirring sugar into a beaker of warm water, the sugar dissolving and disappearing, lab bench with salt, sand, flour, and oil jars, clear before-and-after beakers

choices.label: A. In a sugar solution, sugar is the solute that dissolves in water, which is the solvent
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ In a solution, the solute is the substance that dissolves (sugar), and the solvent is the substance that does the dissolving (water). Water is called the 'universal solvent' because it can dissolve more substances than any other liquid. The solute particles spread evenly throughout the solvent.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. When sugar dissolves in water, the sugar disappears and is destroyed
choices.feedback: 💡 The sugar does not disappear — it is still there! When sugar dissolves, its particles break apart and spread evenly among the water particles. You can prove the sugar is still there by tasting the water (sweet!) or by evaporating the water — the sugar crystals will reappear. Dissolving is NOT destroying.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: C. The solvent is always the substance that is present in a smaller amount
choices.feedback: 💡 Actually, the solvent is usually the substance present in the LARGER amount — it is the one doing the dissolving. The solute is the smaller amount that gets dissolved. In salt water, water (the larger amount) is the solvent, and salt (the smaller amount) is the solute.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: D. A solution is a heterogeneous mixture because it has two different substances
choices.feedback: 💡 A solution is actually a homogeneous mixture! Even though it has two (or more) substances, the solute particles are so tiny and evenly spread that every part of the solution looks and tastes the same. You cannot see the individual sugar particles in sugar water — it is perfectly uniform.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

rounds.situation: Professor Beaker announces a competition: 'Which team can dissolve a sugar cube the fastest — WITHOUT heating it?' He places identical sugar cubes and identical beakers of cold water at each bench. 'You can stir, crush, or do anything else you can think of. But the water stays cold! Ready... set... think!' Sameer starts calculating while Meera reaches for a mortar and pestle.
rounds.goal: Discover all the factors that speed up dissolving and win the dissolving race.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creative problem-solving: There are multiple ways to speed up dissolving. The best scientists consider ALL options before choosing.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Besides heating, what three things can you do to make something dissolve faster? Why does each one work?
rounds.image_prompt: Students racing to dissolve sugar cubes in cold water, one team crushing sugar, another stirring vigorously, another using more water, excited competition atmosphere

choices.label: A. Stirring, heating, and crushing a solute into smaller pieces all speed up dissolving
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Three main factors speed up dissolving: (1) Stirring moves fresh solvent to the solute surface. (2) Heating makes solvent particles move faster, colliding with solute particles more often. (3) Crushing the solute increases the surface area, so more solute is exposed to the solvent at once.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: B. Cooling a solution always makes the solute dissolve faster
choices.feedback: 💡 For most solids, cooling actually slows down dissolving! Hot water dissolves sugar faster than cold water because the water molecules have more energy and collide with sugar particles more often. However, gases are different — cold water can actually dissolve more gas than hot water (think of fizzy cold soda).

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: C. The size of the solute particles does not affect how fast they dissolve
choices.feedback: 💡 Particle size matters a lot! Crushing sugar into a fine powder makes it dissolve much faster than a whole sugar cube. This is because smaller pieces have more surface area exposed to the water. More surface area means more contact between solute and solvent, which means faster dissolving.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: D. Once you stir a solution, the dissolving stops as soon as you stop stirring
choices.feedback: 💡 Dissolving does not stop when stirring stops! Stirring speeds it up, but dissolving continues even without stirring because the solvent particles are always moving and colliding with the solute. A sugar cube left in still water will eventually dissolve completely — it just takes longer without stirring.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

rounds.round_title: Week 5: Saturation — When No More Will Dissolve
rounds.situation: Professor Beaker keeps adding spoonful after spoonful of salt to a beaker of water, stirring each time. Suddenly, the salt stops dissolving — grains just sit at the bottom no matter how much you stir. 'The solution is now SATURATED,' he announces. 'The water cannot hold any more salt. But what if we heat it up? Or try a different substance?' Time to investigate solubility limits!
rounds.goal: Understand saturation, solubility limits, and how temperature affects how much dissolves.
rounds.coaching_moment: Patience and precision: Finding the exact saturation point requires adding tiny amounts and waiting. Rushing gives inaccurate results.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why can hot water dissolve more sugar than cold water? What happens to the extra sugar when the hot solution cools down?
rounds.image_prompt: Beaker with undissolved salt crystals sitting at the bottom of a clear solution, student adding one more spoonful, dissolved and undissolved salt clearly visible

choices.label: A. A saturated solution cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A saturated solution has dissolved the maximum amount of solute possible at that temperature. If you add more sugar to already-saturated sugar water, the extra sugar just sits at the bottom undissolved. Warming the solution can increase solubility, allowing more solute to dissolve.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. You can always dissolve unlimited amounts of solute in any solvent
choices.feedback: 💡 There is a limit! Every solvent can only dissolve a certain amount of solute at a given temperature. Once that limit is reached, the solution is saturated and no more will dissolve. Try adding spoon after spoon of sugar to a cold glass of water — eventually, the sugar just piles up at the bottom.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. Raising the temperature of a solution always makes it less saturated with every solute
choices.feedback: 💡 For most solid solutes, yes — warming increases solubility so the solution can dissolve more. But for gases, it is the opposite! Warm water holds LESS dissolved gas than cold water. This is why a warm soda goes flat faster — the CO2 gas escapes more easily from warm liquid.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. If sugar settles to the bottom of a glass of water, the water is unsaturated
choices.feedback: 💡 If solid sugar is sitting undissolved at the bottom, the solution above it is actually saturated! An unsaturated solution would still be able to dissolve more sugar. When you see undissolved solute at the bottom, it means the water has reached its maximum capacity and cannot absorb any more.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.round_title: Week 6: Filtering — Separating Solids from Liquids
rounds.situation: Professor Beaker holds up a murky beaker of muddy water. 'This contains sand, clay, and dissolved salt,' he says. 'How do we get clean water from this mess? FILTERING is our first separation technique!' He demonstrates folding filter paper into a cone, placing it in a funnel, and pouring the mixture through. The liquid that drips through — the filtrate — is much clearer, but is it pure?
rounds.goal: Master the technique of filtering and understand what it can and cannot separate.
rounds.coaching_moment: Understanding limitations: Filtering catches solid particles but dissolved substances pass right through. Knowing what a technique CANNOT do is as important as knowing what it can.
rounds.reflection_prompt: After filtering muddy salt water, the filtrate is clear — but is it pure water? How would you test?
rounds.image_prompt: Close-up of a filter funnel with filter paper, murky water being poured in, clear filtrate dripping into a clean beaker below, student hands pouring carefully

choices.label: A. Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid by passing it through filter paper
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Filtration works because the filter paper has tiny holes that let liquid particles through but trap larger solid particles. The liquid that passes through is called the filtrate, and the solid left behind is called the residue. This is how coffee makers work — water passes through but coffee grounds stay behind!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. Filtration can separate salt from water because the salt particles get trapped in the filter
choices.feedback: 💡 Filtration cannot separate dissolved substances! When salt dissolves in water, the salt particles become so tiny they pass right through filter paper along with the water. You would need evaporation to separate dissolved salt from water. Filtration only works for insoluble solids like sand, mud, or chalk.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. The solid trapped in the filter paper is called the filtrate
choices.feedback: 💡 You have the terms swapped! The filtrate is the liquid that passes THROUGH the filter. The residue is the solid that stays BEHIND in the filter paper. An easy trick: filtRATE = what goes thROUGH. The residue resides (stays) in the filter.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. Smaller filter paper holes always give better results, so you should use the finest filter possible
choices.feedback: 💡 Smaller holes are not always better! Very fine filters can clog quickly and take a very long time. The right choice depends on the particle size you need to separate. For sand in water, regular filter paper works great. For bacteria, you need special micro-filters. Scientists match the filter to the job.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: EMERGENCY! The school's water supply has been contaminated — tests show elevated levels of sediment and dissolved minerals. The water is not safe to drink until it is purified. The school calls your chemistry class for help! Professor Beaker says: 'This is a real-world challenge. Can you use what you have learned about mixtures and separation to help purify the water?' The whole school is counting on you!
rounds.goal: Apply your separation skills to help purify contaminated school water.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Real-world problems do not come with instructions. You must apply everything you know, stay calm, and work methodically to solve them.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does water purification require MULTIPLE separation techniques and not just one?
rounds.image_prompt: Students urgently working to filter and purify murky water in the chemistry lab, multiple filtration stations set up, teacher supervising, school water crisis

choices.label: A. Clean drinking water requires multiple purification steps: filtering, then disinfecting to kill germs
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Water purification uses multiple steps because different methods remove different contaminants. Filtering removes solid particles (mud, sand). Then chemicals like chlorine or UV light kill bacteria and viruses. Some plants also use sedimentation (letting particles settle) and activated carbon (removing chemicals). Each step handles a different problem!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.
skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: B. Filtering water through a cloth makes it completely safe to drink
choices.feedback: 💡 This is a dangerous misconception! Cloth filtering only removes large particles like dirt and debris. It does NOT remove bacteria, viruses, or dissolved chemicals that can make you very sick. Safe drinking water requires additional steps like boiling, chlorination, or UV treatment to kill invisible germs.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: C. Clear water is always safe to drink because it has no impurities
choices.feedback: 💡 Clear water can still be very unsafe! Dissolved chemicals, bacteria, and viruses are invisible to the naked eye. A glass of water can look perfectly clear but contain harmful lead, arsenic, or disease-causing bacteria. That is why water treatment plants test water carefully — you cannot judge safety by appearance alone.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: D. Boiling water only makes it hot but does not remove any impurities
choices.feedback: 💡 Boiling is actually an important purification step! When you boil water, the high temperature (100°C) kills most bacteria, viruses, and parasites that can cause disease. However, boiling does not remove dissolved chemicals or heavy metals. That is why it is one step in purification, not the only step.

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

rounds.round_title: Week 8: Evaporation — Getting the Dissolved Stuff Back
rounds.situation: After the water crisis, Professor Beaker asks: 'We removed dissolved salt from water by distillation. But what if we WANT the salt? What if we need to recover the dissolved substance?' He heats a dish of salt water gently. 'Watch what happens as the water evaporates...' Slowly, white crystals appear in the dish. 'Evaporation lets us recover dissolved solids!'
rounds.goal: Use evaporation to separate dissolved solids from solutions and recover them.
rounds.coaching_moment: Patience: Evaporation is slow and requires patience, but it recovers valuable substances that filtering cannot. Sometimes the slow method is the right method.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Evaporation recovers the dissolved solid. But what happens to the water? Where does it go?
rounds.image_prompt: Evaporating dish on a tripod over low flame, salt crystals forming as water evaporates, student watching closely with magnifying glass, steam rising gently

choices.label: A. Evaporation can separate a dissolved solid from a liquid by heating until the liquid turns to gas
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ When you heat a salt solution, the water evaporates (turns to gas and escapes) but the dissolved salt cannot evaporate — it stays behind as solid crystals. This is how sea salt is harvested in many countries: seawater is left in shallow pools, the sun evaporates the water, and salt crystals remain!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. When salt water evaporates, both the salt and water turn into gas together
choices.feedback: 💡 Only the water evaporates, not the salt! Salt has a much higher boiling point (1,413°C) than water (100°C). When you heat salt water, the water molecules have enough energy to escape as gas, but the salt particles do not. This is exactly why evaporation works as a separation technique.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. Evaporation is the best method to separate sand from water
choices.feedback: 💡 Evaporation would work but is wasteful and slow! Filtration is much better for separating sand from water because sand is insoluble — it does not dissolve. Just pour through filter paper and the sand stays behind. Evaporation is best for recovering dissolved substances like salt. Always choose the simplest effective method!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. After evaporating salt water, you get back more salt than you originally added
choices.feedback: 💡 You get back exactly the same amount of salt you started with! No new salt is created during evaporation. Mass is conserved — the salt was always there, just dissolved and invisible. If you dissolved 10 grams of salt, you will recover 10 grams of salt crystals after evaporation.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.situation: Professor Beaker sets up an impressive apparatus — a flask, a delivery tube, and a collecting beaker surrounded by cold water. 'Distillation combines evaporation AND condensation to separate a dissolved solid from a liquid — and keep BOTH!' he explains. 'The liquid evaporates, travels through the tube, cools down and condenses back into pure liquid. This is how we make pure water from sea water!'
rounds.goal: Understand and perform distillation to produce pure water from a solution.
rounds.coaching_moment: Connecting concepts: Distillation uses evaporation and condensation together — two processes you already know. Combining known techniques to solve new problems is advanced thinking.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How is distillation different from just boiling? Why do we need the cooling tube?
rounds.image_prompt: Distillation apparatus in a school lab — round flask on burner, bent delivery tube leading to a collection beaker in ice water, steam condensing into pure water drops

choices.label: A. Distillation separates liquids by heating to boil one liquid first, then cooling its vapor back to liquid
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Distillation uses differences in boiling points. When you heat a mixture of two liquids, the one with the lower boiling point boils first and turns to vapor. This vapor travels through a condenser where it cools back into a pure liquid and is collected separately. This is how we get pure water from seawater!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. Distillation works by filtering one liquid from another using special paper
choices.feedback: 💡 You cannot filter one liquid from another — both pass through filter paper! Distillation uses heat, not filtering. It works by boiling: the liquid with the lower boiling point evaporates first, travels through a cooling tube (condenser), and is collected as a separate pure liquid. It is about boiling points, not particle size.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. In distillation, the liquid that boils at a higher temperature evaporates first
choices.feedback: 💡 The liquid with the LOWER boiling point evaporates first! It needs less heat energy to boil. In a water-alcohol mixture, alcohol (boiling point 78°C) evaporates before water (boiling point 100°C). This is the whole principle behind distillation — different boiling points allow separation.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. Distillation and evaporation are exactly the same separation technique
choices.feedback: 💡 They are related but different! In evaporation, the vapor escapes into the air and you only keep the solid left behind. In distillation, the vapor is collected by cooling it back to a liquid. Distillation recovers BOTH substances, while evaporation only recovers the solid. Distillation is like evaporation + condensation.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.situation: Professor Beaker draws a dot of black marker on a strip of filter paper and dips the bottom edge in water. As the water climbs up the paper, the black dot begins to separate into different colors — blue, red, purple! 'This is chromatography,' he announces. 'Black ink is actually a MIXTURE of several dyes. Chromatography separates them because each dye is carried by the water at a different speed.'
rounds.goal: Perform chromatography to separate mixtures of dyes and identify their components.
rounds.coaching_moment: Hidden complexity: What looks simple (black ink) can be surprisingly complex (a mixture of dyes). Never assume something is simple just because it looks that way.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do different dyes travel different distances up the paper? What does this tell us about the dye molecules?
rounds.image_prompt: Close-up of chromatography paper strips showing separated colors from black ink — bands of blue, red, yellow, purple climbing up the paper, water reaching the top

choices.label: A. Chromatography separates mixtures based on how differently each substance travels through a material
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ In chromatography, a solvent (like water) moves through a material (like filter paper) carrying dissolved substances with it. Different substances travel at different speeds because they are attracted to the paper differently. This separates them into visible bands. Black ink, for example, is often a mixture of blue, red, and yellow dyes!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.creativity: Not settling for the obvious solution builds creative problem-solving.

choices.label: B. Chromatography only works on colored substances and cannot separate colorless ones
choices.feedback: 💡 Chromatography works on colorless substances too! Scientists use special detection methods like UV light or chemical staining to see colorless bands. Chromatography is used to detect drugs in blood samples, analyze food additives, and even solve crimes — most of these substances are colorless.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. In chromatography, all substances in a mixture travel the same distance
choices.feedback: 💡 If they all traveled the same distance, nothing would be separated! The whole point of chromatography is that different substances travel different distances. Some are more attracted to the paper (move slowly) while others are more attracted to the solvent (move quickly). This difference in speed is what separates them.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. Chromatography requires expensive equipment and cannot be done in a school lab
choices.feedback: 💡 Paper chromatography is one of the simplest experiments you can do! All you need is filter paper (or even a coffee filter), water, and a marker pen. Put a dot of ink on the paper, dip the edge in water, and watch the colors separate. It is a beautiful and easy experiment you can try at home!

skill_explanation.creativity: Thinking outside the box leads to more original solutions.

rounds.situation: Professor Beaker places a bowl of mixed iron filings, sand, salt, and rice on each bench. 'This mixture has four different substances. To separate them ALL, you will need to use MULTIPLE techniques in the right ORDER,' he says, holding up a magnet. 'This is magnetic separation — the simplest technique for any mixture containing magnetic materials. But what order do you use for the rest?'
rounds.goal: Use magnetic separation and plan a multi-step separation strategy.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic planning: Choosing the RIGHT separation technique in the RIGHT ORDER is critical. A good plan saves time, materials, and produces purer results.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why must you separate the iron filings FIRST before adding water? What would go wrong if you dissolved the salt first?
rounds.image_prompt: Student holding a magnet over a bowl of mixed iron filings, sand, salt, and rice — iron filings jumping to the magnet, other materials staying behind

choices.label: A. A magnet can separate iron filings from sand because iron is magnetic but sand is not
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Magnetic separation works because some materials (like iron, nickel, and cobalt) are attracted to magnets while others are not. When you pass a magnet over a sand-iron mixture, only the iron filings stick to the magnet, leaving the sand behind. Recycling plants use giant magnets to separate steel cans from other rubbish!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. All metals are magnetic and can be separated using a magnet
choices.feedback: 💡 Not all metals are magnetic! Only iron, nickel, cobalt, and their alloys (like steel) are attracted to magnets. Aluminium, copper, gold, and silver are NOT magnetic. That is why you cannot pick up an aluminium can with a fridge magnet. Magnetic separation only works for magnetic materials.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: C. Magnetic separation is the only method needed to separate any mixture of solids
choices.feedback: 💡 Magnetic separation only works when one component is magnetic! For a mixture of salt and sand, you would need dissolving + filtering + evaporation. For a mixture of colored inks, you need chromatography. The key to science is choosing the RIGHT method for each specific mixture.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: D. When you separate iron filings with a magnet, the iron changes into a different substance
choices.feedback: 💡 The iron stays the same substance! All separation methods are physical processes — they separate substances without changing what they are. The iron filings are still iron, and the sand is still sand. No new substances are created. This is a key difference between physical separation and chemical reactions.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

rounds.situation: CRISIS! During a routine experiment, a bottle of copper sulfate solution tips over and spills across two benches, mixing with iron filings, sand, and other chemicals. The blue liquid is spreading and some students are panicking. Professor Beaker shouts: 'Do not touch it! Copper sulfate can irritate skin. We need to contain this spill, clean it up safely, and — if possible — recover the copper sulfate so it is not wasted. This is a real lab emergency!'
rounds.goal: Handle the chemical spill safely and use separation techniques to clean up and recover materials.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience under pressure: Emergencies test everything you have learned. Staying calm, applying the right techniques in the right order, and keeping everyone safe is the ultimate test.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How do the separation techniques you learned — filtering, magnetic separation, evaporation — apply to cleaning up a chemical spill?
rounds.image_prompt: Chemistry lab with blue copper sulfate solution spilling across benches, students stepping back, teacher directing cleanup, safety goggles and gloves visible

choices.label: A. A concentrated solution has a large amount of solute dissolved in the solvent compared to a dilute one
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Concentration describes how much solute is dissolved in a given amount of solvent. A concentrated solution has lots of solute (like very strong, sweet lemonade with lots of sugar). A dilute solution has very little solute (like weak, watery lemonade). You can dilute a solution by adding more solvent!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.
skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: B. Dilute and concentrated solutions of the same substance are completely different chemicals
choices.feedback: 💡 They contain the same chemicals, just in different proportions! Dilute lemon juice and concentrated lemon juice both contain citric acid and water. The concentrated version just has more citric acid per volume. You can turn concentrated into dilute by adding more water (solvent).

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. Adding more solvent to a solution makes it more concentrated
choices.feedback: 💡 Adding more solvent makes the solution more DILUTE, not concentrated! When you add water to orange squash, it becomes weaker and more watery. The same amount of solute is now spread across more solvent. To make it more concentrated, you would need to add more solute or remove some solvent.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. A saturated solution and a concentrated solution are always the same thing
choices.feedback: 💡 Not the same! A concentrated solution has lots of solute, but it could still dissolve more. A saturated solution has dissolved the absolute maximum — no more can dissolve. A solution can be concentrated without being saturated. Saturation is the limit; concentration just means there is a lot of solute.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.situation: With the Lab Showcase one week away, Professor Beaker assigns the ultimate challenge: 'Design and build a complete water purification system that takes dirty river water and produces clean, clear drinking water. Use EVERY separation technique you have learned.' He shows a bottle of murky river water containing mud, sand, leaves, dissolved salts, and bacteria. 'This is your final exam — in hands-on form!'
rounds.goal: Design and build a complete multi-stage water purification system using all separation techniques.
rounds.coaching_moment: Integration: This project combines filtering, evaporation, distillation, and more. The ability to integrate multiple skills into one solution is the hallmark of a true scientist.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What is the order of purification steps, and why does each step come where it does?
rounds.image_prompt: Students building a multi-stage water purification system — sedimentation tank, gravel filter, sand filter, charcoal filter, UV light, collection vessel, murky to clear water

choices.label: A. A multi-stage water purifier uses sedimentation, filtration, and disinfection in sequence
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Real water treatment plants use multiple stages: (1) Sedimentation lets heavy particles settle to the bottom. (2) Filtration removes smaller suspended particles. (3) Disinfection (chlorine or UV) kills bacteria and viruses. Some plants add activated carbon to remove chemicals and bad taste. Each stage targets different contaminants!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.
skill_explanation.creativity: Exploring an unconventional approach shows creative thinking.

choices.label: B. Just boiling water removes all impurities including dissolved chemicals and heavy metals
choices.feedback: 💡 Boiling kills germs but does NOT remove dissolved chemicals or heavy metals! If water contains dissolved lead or pesticides, boiling it actually makes it MORE concentrated (because some water evaporates but the chemicals stay). For complete purification, you need filtration and sometimes distillation or activated carbon.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. The order of purification steps does not matter — you can do them in any sequence
choices.feedback: 💡 The order matters a lot! If you disinfect before filtering, new germs from unfiltered particles could re-contaminate the water. Sedimentation should come first (removes big stuff), then filtration (removes small stuff), then disinfection (kills germs in the now-clean water). Working from big to small to invisible is the most efficient approach.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. All the water on Earth is naturally pure and does not need any purification
choices.feedback: 💡 Natural water almost always contains impurities! River water has dissolved minerals, bacteria, mud, and sometimes pollution. Even rainwater picks up gases and dust as it falls. Groundwater dissolves minerals from rocks. Water purification is essential to make water safe for drinking — about 2 billion people worldwide lack access to safe water.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.situation: Lab Showcase day is here! The school hall is transformed into a chemistry exhibition. Parents, teachers, and students from other grades are visiting. Your bench displays your water purification system, chromatography art, crystal collection, and separation technique chart. Professor Beaker opens with a proud speech: 'These students can now take any mixture in the world and figure out how to separate it. They are true chemists!' It is your moment to shine!
rounds.goal: Showcase your separation skills and make Lab Showcase a triumph for your team.
rounds.coaching_moment: Confidence: You have earned this moment through 13 weeks of mixing, separating, and discovering. Trust your knowledge and share it with pride.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Looking back at Week 1, how much has your understanding of mixtures changed? What was the most surprising thing you learned?
rounds.image_prompt: School science exhibition hall with student booths, parents visiting, colorful displays showing water purification systems and chromatography art, proud students presenting

choices.label: A. Suspensions are cloudy mixtures where large particles eventually settle, unlike solutions and colloids
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ There are three types of liquid mixtures: Solutions (clear, particles too tiny to see, never settle — like salt water). Colloids (slightly cloudy, medium particles, do not settle — like milk). Suspensions (cloudy, large particles that eventually settle to the bottom — like muddy water). Shaking a suspension mixes it temporarily!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.creativity: Looking at the problem from a new angle demonstrates creativity.

choices.label: B. A colloid is the same as a solution because both look clear and uniform
choices.feedback: 💡 Colloids and solutions look similar but are different! You can tell them apart with the Tyndall effect: shine a light beam through them. In a solution, the light passes straight through. In a colloid (like milk or fog), the light beam becomes visible because it scatters off the suspended particles.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. Muddy water is a solution because the mud is mixed evenly with the water
choices.feedback: 💡 Muddy water is a suspension, not a solution! The mud particles are large and heavy. If you let muddy water stand still, the mud slowly settles to the bottom — solutions never do this. Also, you can filter mud out of water, but you cannot filter salt out of salt water. Settling is the key sign of a suspension.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. All separation techniques we learned work equally well on any type of mixture
choices.feedback: 💡 Each separation technique works best for specific types of mixtures! Filtration: insoluble solids from liquids. Evaporation: dissolved solids from liquids. Distillation: separating liquids. Chromatography: dissolved colored/colorless substances. Magnetic separation: magnetic from non-magnetic. Choosing the right method is a key science skill!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

glossary_terms.definition: Two or more substances mixed together but not chemically combined. The substances keep their own properties and can be separated by physical methods.
A special type of mixture where one substance (the solute) dissolves completely in another (the solvent). Solutions look clear because the dissolved particles are too small to see.
The substance that dissolves in a solvent. In salt water, the salt is the solute. It breaks into particles too small to see.
The substance that does the dissolving. Water is called the 'universal solvent' because it dissolves more substances than any other liquid.
The process of a solute breaking into tiny particles and spreading evenly throughout a solvent. The solute seems to disappear but is still present.
The point at which no more solute can dissolve in a solvent at a given temperature. A saturated solution cannot hold any more dissolved substance.
A separation technique that uses a barrier (like filter paper) to trap solid particles while allowing liquids to pass through. It cannot remove dissolved substances.
A separation technique where the liquid is heated until it turns to gas, leaving the dissolved solid behind. Used to recover dissolved substances like salt from salt water.
A separation technique combining evaporation and condensation to separate a dissolved solid from a liquid while keeping BOTH. Used to make pure water from sea water.
A separation technique that separates dissolved substances based on how fast they travel through a material (like paper). Used to analyze dyes, inks, and food colorings.
Using a magnet to separate magnetic materials (like iron) from non-magnetic materials. Used in recycling plants to separate steel from other waste.
The liquid that passes through a filter. It may look clear but can still contain dissolved substances that were too small for the filter to trap.

endings.title: Separation Specialist
endings.message: You have achieved mastery in the Mixtures & Solutions Kitchen! Your separation techniques are extraordinary, your safety record is impeccable, and your water purification system amazed the entire school. Professor Beaker nominates you for the District Science Award, and the local newspaper features your Lab Showcase project. You have proven that with the right knowledge, any mixture can be separated!

endings.title: Skilled Young Chemist
endings.message: You have become a skilled young chemist with solid knowledge of mixtures and separation! Your Lab Showcase project demonstrates real competence in separating and analyzing substances. Professor Beaker is proud and says you are ready for the advanced chemistry module. Your skills are genuine and your future in science is bright!

endings.title: Lab Regular
endings.message: You completed the Mixtures & Solutions Kitchen program with mixed results. Some weeks were great and others were tough, but you stuck with it and learned the basics of mixtures and separation. Professor Beaker says there is always next semester to improve, and the foundation you built will serve you well!

endings.title: Struggling Student
endings.message: The Mixtures & Solutions Kitchen was a tough journey for you. Many of the techniques were confusing, and the experiments did not always work. But you did not give up. Professor Beaker arranges extra sessions and says: 'The students who struggle the most often end up understanding the deepest.' Your story is not over!

endings.title: Lab Probation
endings.message: Due to repeated safety violations and low safety awareness, Professor Beaker has placed you on Lab Probation. You can only observe experiments until you pass the safety certification. Safety around chemicals is non-negotiable. Bubble the mascot has volunteered to tutor you. This setback is temporary — learn from it and come back stronger!

questions.question: What are the three states of matter?
questions.explanation: The three common states of matter are solid, liquid, and gas.

questions.question: What happens to particles when a solid is heated?

choices.text: They vibrate faster and spread apart

questions.explanation: Heating gives particles more energy, making them vibrate faster and eventually change state.

questions.question: A chemical change is different from a physical change because:
questions.explanation: Chemical changes produce new substances with different properties.
